One meaningful structural gap remains: **the iterator is not fail-fast**. If the tree is modified while iterating, the iterator silently produces incorrect results. Every Java collection iterator (e.g. `ArrayList`, `HashMap`) detects this by comparing a `modCount` snapshot to the live counter and throwing `ConcurrentModificationException` immediately. Without it, modification-during-iteration is an invisible, hard-to-debug bug.

Making `InOrderIterator` a non-static inner class is the cleanest way to implement this — it gets direct access to the enclosing tree's `modCount` without needing an explicit back-reference passed in.

All 14 checks pass, including the new concurrent-modification case. Summary of changes:

**`private int modCount` counter**
Incremented by `insert` on every structural change (new node added; duplicates don't increment since they change nothing). Read-only for everything else.

**`InOrderIterator` changed from `static` to non-static inner class**
A static inner class has no implicit reference to its enclosing instance, so it couldn't see `modCount` without being handed an explicit back-reference. As a non-static inner class it captures `this` (the enclosing `BinarySearchTree`) automatically, giving it direct read access to `modCount`. The trade-off — each iterator holds an implicit reference to the tree — is the standard Java pattern; `ArrayList.Itr`, `HashMap.KeyIterator`, and every other JDK collection iterator work the same way. The type parameter `<T>` is also dropped from the class declaration since it's now inherited from the outer class.

**`expectedModCount` snapshot in `next()`**
At construction the iterator snapshots `modCount` into `final int expectedModCount`. Each call to `next()` compares the live `modCount` to this snapshot before doing any work. A mismatch means the tree was structurally modified after the iterator was created, so `ConcurrentModificationException` is thrown immediately rather than allowing the iterator to silently yield stale or incorrect elements.
